title: How do you design a puff print that stays readable on a hoodie?
description: Prepare raised artwork at actual size, test the smallest gaps and review a puff print in the position where it will be worn.
author: BEWE4R team
intro: Puff print gives selected parts of an artwork a raised surface. It works well when the relief itself has a visual purpose. On a hoodie wordmark, for example, a broad raised letter can catch side light while a flat outline keeps the edges clear. Before approving the effect, look at the smallest gap you need to keep open.

toc.text: Test the position on a body
Build an approval record the printer can repeat
What if the puff print is meant to sit next to flat lettering?
When is a second trial worthwhile?

bodyHtml:
Decide which parts should rise

Give the decorator separate artwork layers for the raised and flat areas. A single mockup with a drop shadow shows the designer’s intention but leaves the print team guessing where the physical relief begins. Mark the finished width and the garment size used in the drawing.

For a script logo, the space between adjacent strokes can matter as much as the stroke width. Ask for a small trial with the original lettering and a version with slightly more space. Inspect both on the same base fabric in normal light, at the distance a person would usually see the garment.

Test the position on a body

A raised motif across a pocket edge or near a crease may change appearance when the wearer sits. Place a paper outline on the finished sample first. Mark its top edge from a named seam and review the design with the hood up and down. A large upper-back wordmark can disappear behind the hood even when its print is flawless.

Build an approval record the printer can repeat

RecordDetail to capture
ArtworkWhich shapes rise, the final width and the accepted lettering revision
GroundFabric reference, colour and surface finish
AppearanceFront view for legibility and side-lit view for relief
Care reviewCondition before and after the agreed care procedure, with any lifting or surface changes noted

Keep the physical trial. A side-lit photograph can exaggerate height, while a straight-on image can make it disappear. If two buyers disagree about the result, compare both to the same physical sample under the same lighting.

What if the puff print is meant to sit next to flat lettering?

Ask the printer to prepare one trial containing the raised section and the flat word at their final spacing. Look across the sample from the side and read it from the front. If the raised edge obscures a letter, mark the gap on the artwork and retest that junction. A puff-only swatch cannot answer this design question.

When is a second trial worthwhile?

If the letters read well but merge after raising, revise the artwork before changing the whole garment. If the logo is clear on the trial and poorly placed on the hoodie, revise placement instead. Separating those decisions makes it easier to approve what already works. View BEWE4R’s puff print examples and send the part of the artwork you want raised.
